title: Nehemiah 2:17–20
context: Nehemiah 2:17–20 records Nehemiah’s appeal to the people to rebuild the wall so that they will no longer be a reproach, his testimony to the good hand of God and the king’s words, and the people’s response, “Let’s rise up and build.” Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arabian ridicule them and ask whether they are rebelling against the king, a charge that recalls the earlier accusation in Ezra 4:12 that the Jews were rebuilding “the rebellious and bad city”. Nehemiah answers that the God of heaven will prosper them, that they as his servants will build, and that the opponents have no portion, right, or memorial in Jerusalem. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: God’s people take up his work with confidence in him, and opposition does not decide the outcome.

verses.text: Then I said to them, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burned with fire. Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah tells them they see the bad situation, Jerusalem lying waste and its gates burned, and he calls, “Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.” He speaks as one of them.

Arminian readers note the inclusive we, and they see Nehemiah inviting a willing, shared response from the people rather than issuing an order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the disgrace of Jerusalem is also a reproach to God’s name (compare 1:3), and they see the call to build as a call to restore the honor of the city God had chosen.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about honest assessment and a summons to shared work for the good of God’s people.

verses.text: I told them about the hand of my God which was good on me, and also about the king’s words that he had spoken to me. They said, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.
verses.arminianNotes:
He tells them about the hand of his God that was good on him and about the king’s words, and they say, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthen their hands for the good work.

Arminian readers see the people responding freely and wholeheartedly once they hear what God has done, and they note the encouragement that testimony brings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Nehemiah’s testimony centers on the good hand of God, and they see the people’s resolve as strengthened by God’s evident work, so that the good work is both God’s and theirs.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: testimony to God’s help encourages his people to take up his work together.

verses.text: But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they ridiculed us and despised us, and said, “What is this thing that you are doing? Will you rebel against the king?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arabian ridicule and despise them, asking, “What is this thing that you are doing? Will you rebel against the king?” The charge of rebellion recalls Ezra 4:12, and Geshem appears again in 6:1.

Arminian readers note that ridicule and accusation are chosen responses of the opponents.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the pattern of opposition to God’s work, which uses mockery and political suspicion, and they note that the charge is false, since Nehemiah has the king’s letters.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and describe the opponents only as the text does.

verses.text: Then I answered them, and said to them, “The God of heaven will prosper us. Therefore we, his servants, will arise and build; but you have no portion, nor right, nor memorial in Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah answers, “The God of heaven will prosper us. Therefore we, his servants, will arise and build; but you have no portion, nor right, nor memorial in Jerusalem.” He grounds the work in God.

Arminian readers note that confidence in God leads to the people’s own determined action, so that divine help and human effort go together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that success is attributed first to the God of heaven, and they see the declaration that the opponents have no portion, right, or memorial in Jerusalem as a statement about covenant belonging in the city, not a general verdict on their persons.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about confident trust in God amid opposition.
